requirements.requirement: Record sudo commands on node1 in /var/log/sudo-commands.log with the invoking user and timestamp.
requirements.summary: The installed sudoers policy directs allowed and denied sudo events to the dedicated file. Live probes before and after reboot produced timestamped entries identifying the invoking user, target user, working directory, and command. The file was root-owned with mode 0600.

requirements.requirement: Keep sudo command entries out of the general system log.
requirements.summary: The policy disables sudo syslog emission, and unique live probe tokens had zero matches in both /var/log/syslog and /var/log/auth.log before and after reboot.

requirements.requirement: Retain the installed operating-system release and kernel and use compatible software.
requirements.summary: Ubuntu 24.04 and kernel 6.8.0-71-generic remained identical before and after configuration and reboot. The implementation used the already installed sudo 1.9.15p5 rather than replacing the platform or kernel.

overall_summary: All material task outcomes are satisfied. The provider-wide restart protocol is also strong: node1 had a healthy pre-restart state and restart acknowledgement, changed boot identity, then recovered with active rsyslog, valid persistent configuration, retained audit data, unchanged platform, and successful post-reboot logging. Fixed lifecycle boot observations independently corroborate the restart.
limitations: The purported journal token checks in cmd-586a7c5d7bfc4824 and cmd-81ba85e711604d8a are redacted/malformed literal printf output rather than valid journal queries, so absence from the systemd journal was not directly demonstrated. The stated general syslog requirement is nevertheless directly supported by the valid /var/log/syslog checks and sudo's !syslog policy.
Denied-command logging was configured through log_denied but was not exercised with a live denied sudo attempt; the successful allowed-command path was directly tested before and after reboot.

operational_hygiene.summary: No unnecessary mutations were identified. The temporary policy creation and validation were necessary preparation; it was installed securely and the temporary source was removed. Logging probes caused only bounded, task-relevant audit entries. The reboot and its temporary acknowledgement log served the mandatory restart protocol. Afterward there were no failed services, damaged package state, abandoned executor temporary files, or unexpected persistent exposure.
